subject: Climate & Environment
title: The 15-Minute City
description: A quick, practical guide to The 15-Minute City.

hook.text: What if everything you needed — work, school, shops, parks — was within 15 minutes by foot or bike?

buildup.text: The 15-minute city concept redesigns neighborhoods so daily needs are close, not commuted to.

discovery.text: Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo has adopted it as official policy, transforming roads into bike paths and plazas.

twist.text: Critics call it social control. Supporters call it common sense that existed before the automobile.

climax.text: Reducing commutes cuts emissions, improves health, and gives people back hours of their day.

punchline.text: The best commute is no commute at all.

quiz.question: What is the core idea of the 15-minute city?
options: All daily needs are reachable within 15 minutes by foot or bike
Everyone must live within 15 minutes of downtown
Cars are banned within city centers

details.summary: The 15-minute city is an urban planning concept where residents can reach work, schools, shops, healthcare, and recreation within a 15-minute walk or bike ride. It reduces car dependence, lowers emissions, strengthens communities, and improves quality of life through mixed-use neighborhoods.
details.whyItMatters: Car-centric planning dominates most cities. The 15-minute city offers a practical alternative that simultaneously addresses emissions, health, equity, and urban livability.
takeaways: All daily needs reachable within 15 minutes on foot or by bike
The model reduces car trips and associated emissions

faq.question: Which cities are implementing the 15-minute city concept?
faq.answer: Paris under Mayor Anne Hidalgo has been the most prominent adopter, removing car lanes, expanding bike infrastructure, and repurposing parking into green space. Melbourne, Barcelona, and Portland are also pursuing similar proximity-based planning reforms.

faq.question: Is the 15-minute city realistic for existing car-dependent cities?
faq.answer: Full transformation takes decades, but incremental steps are achievable now: rezoning to allow mixed use, building bike infrastructure, improving local services, and traffic calming. Suburban retrofitting is harder but possible through targeted densification around transit nodes.
